headline: Trump's plan for Europe's nationalists has not worked
lead: Transatlantic alliance between Maga movement, European right-wing populists in crisis: Three reasons
seo_title: Trump and Europe's right wing: why the alliance is in crisis
social_title: Trump's plan for Europe's nationalists has not worked
print_title: Trump's plan for Europe's nationalists has not worked
print_subtitle: The transatlantic alliance between the Maga movement and European right-wing populists is in crisis for three reasons
summary_bullets_en: Europe's right-wing populists are increasingly distancing themselves from Donald Trump due to economic dependence on the EU and disagreements over geopolitical issues.
Disputes include Trump's tariff policies, individual political choices, and his stances on Russia and Ukraine, which threaten European security interests.
While the ideological connection between Europe's right-wing and the MAGA movement remains, Trump's popularity in Europe has significantly declined.

body.caption: Turning away: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and President Donald Trump.

body.text: Europe is a continent in decline. Its aging population is being overrun by migrants, and governments in its capitals suppress free speech and miss out on future technologies, according to Trump's description of Europe, which he published in the National Security Strategy (NSS) late last year. It is also Elon Musk's assessment; he predicts a civil war in Europe in an interview with the «Economist».

Europe, the NSS continues, is on the path to «civilizational extinction.» However, the U.S. would not simply accept this, as the old continent remains «strategically and culturally indispensable» for the country. Therefore, resistance in individual nations must be supported, the NSS states. This means the U.S. should ally itself «with the patriotic parties of Europe.»
Shared ideology no longer a bond

This was an offer that delighted those it addressed: the AfD in Germany, the Rassemblement National in France, the Fratelli d’Italia, the Spanish Vox, Nigel Farage's Reform UK, and not least Viktor Orbán and his Fidesz, who are firmly rooted in the Maga movement.

Eight months later, the tide has turned. European nationalists and right-wing populists have distanced themselves from Trump, even though their view of the continent aligns with his. They particularly share the idea that «European civilization» (implicitly Christian and white-coded) is at stake, these groups say. But economic and geopolitical rifts have opened up that are insurmountable for the foreseeable future.
Three reasons are decisive for this.
1. Economy

Economically, ruling far-right parties depend on the EU. This is most obvious in Italy's case. Italy benefits most from the EU's COVID Recovery Fund. It receives nearly 20 billion euros from it, mainly for infrastructure projects. This creates an important economic link between the Fratelli and Brussels, particularly as the funds' use is monitored there and their disbursement is tied to reforms.

Conversely, American tariff policy is a problem for Italy. Important sectors are affected, including the machinery industry, the fashion industry and the food industry. The Italian business association Confindustria warns of the loss of tens of thousands of jobs.

It is no wonder Prime Minister Meloni describes Trump's tariff policy as a mistake. She must place her hopes in the EU, which has negotiating power thanks to the cumulative trade volumes of its members. Meloni therefore blocked the proposal from her junior coalition partner, Lega leader Matteo Salvini, to negotiate a separate agreement with Washington. Ultimately, 50% of all Italian exports go to the EU, and only 10% to the U.S.
Slovakia and Poland are in a similar situation, where their far-right parties distance themselves from American tariff policy simply out of consideration for their voters.
2. Geopolitics

The geopolitical interest collides with American foreign policy in many European countries. Poland's case is illustrative here. The country is one of the closest allies of the U.S. in Europe, and PiS-affiliated President Karol Nawrocki maintains close ties with Trump and his circle. At the same time, Poland views Russia and its war against Ukraine as an immediate threat.

Accordingly, the Polish far-right party, which aligns with Maga on migration, EU skepticism and anti-woke stances, views Trump's behavior toward Moscow and Kyiv critically. His demonstrative closeness to Putin and his erratic relationship with Zelenskyy are irritating. Nawrocki and the PiS leadership almost naively warned the American president not to «trust Putin.» Trump's weakening of NATO also created distance. No politician can afford to appear as Trump's vassal and jeopardize the country's security.

The war against Iran is another wedge issue. Meloni fell out with Trump after the attack on the Islamic Republic. As everywhere in Europe (and in the U.S.), Trump's military action in the Gulf is unpopular in Italy. Meloni therefore felt compelled to restrict the use of American bases in the country. Trump, who had hoped for much more extensive European support, reacted with a publicly staged withdrawal of affection.

Trump's threat in January to «take» Greenland also produced a consistently negative reaction. It led to a rift. The head of the Danish People's Party had to justify his previous visit to Mar-a-Lago. A party spokesperson even declared the president's demand to be crazy.

The AfD also distanced itself. Party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla said that with his wild-west methods, Trump was breaking his election promise of non-interference. Jordan Bardella, the second-highest official of the Rassemblement National, even considered advocating for the suspension of the trade agreement with Washington. And Nigel Farage dismissed Trump's tariff threats, should Denmark prove unwilling, as «extremely hostile.»
Thus, there is a pan-European interest in territorial integrity and sovereignty, which is also important for far-right parties. This should not be surprising; after all, they are nationalists.
3. Donald Trump

The days are over when European right-wing populists primarily rejoiced about their ally in the White House. Trump's political style annoys and repels. He is perceived as authentic, which is a rare quality among top politicians. But that does not make Trump's unpredictability, his narcissism and his material greed any more likable. Trump's popularity among right-wing parties has continued to decline in recent months.

A few examples: Trump's claim that the British contribution to the Afghanistan war was hardly helpful could not be sugar-coated even by Nigel Farage. His criticism of the Pope in April, saying he did not understand foreign policy, and the subsequent primitive insults against Meloni («begs for a photo with me») were also received extremely poorly in Italy's right-wing camp. The shameless intervention with FIFA President Gianni Infantino in favor of an American soccer player during the World Cup was also poorly received.

In Germany, only 9% of respondents now rate Trump positively; in France it is 15%, and in Italy 8%. And this comes precisely at a moment when far-right parties are gaining support in these countries. The consistent reaction of party leaders is therefore to distance themselves from Trump. Closeness to the American president is a liability for campaigners in Europe.
**Not all bridges burned**

However, this by no means signifies the end of the ideological kinship and relationship cultivation between parties, organizations and media across the Atlantic. While the right-wing, transatlantic milieu in Europe has lost a central figure with the departure of Viktor Orbán, the friendship with the Maga camp in the U.S. continues.

What most strongly connects the movements is their common adversary, the liberal center, both here and there. Ultimately, the damage is also containable, for it has a name: Donald Trump. Meloni is no longer Trump's whisperer. But she remains proud of the author who wrote the foreword for her book «The Vision of Giorgia.» That author is J. D. Vance, the Vice President.
